methodology_note: 2020-2024 figures are NOAA NCEI's official 'Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters' totals (CPI-adjusted to 2024 dollars) for the single costliest qualifying wildfire event(s) of that year -- the same U.S. government dataset used for hurricanes, floods, etc. NOAA discontinued ongoing updates to this product after the 2024 edition, so 2025 and 2026 have no equivalent official figure; those years use third-party estimates flagged below, and are not directly comparable in methodology.

annual.source: AccuWeather preliminary total damage & economic loss estimate
annual.note: NOAA's official tracker was discontinued before 2025, so no directly comparable government figure exists. Estimates for this single event vary enormously by scope: insured-loss-only estimates run $28-40B (Verisk, Swiss Re), while broader total-damage-and-economic-loss estimates (property, business interruption, indirect costs) reach $250-275B (AccuWeather) or as high as $95-164B in UCLA Anderson Forecast's property/capital-loss-only framing. Even the lowest of these estimates exceeds every other year in this chart.

annual.source: State fire agency suppression-cost reports (Colorado, Oregon, Utah)
annual.note: No single billion-dollar wildfire event has been tallied yet in 2026. This figure is suppression cost only (not total economic/property damage) from three states with early public figures: Colorado ~$266M (90-day projection, 4 largest fires), Oregon ~$90.9M (large-fire suppression through July 21), Utah ~$20M (through July 1) -- it excludes every other state and all non-suppression losses, and peak fire season (Aug-Oct) has not happened yet. Nationally, 2026 is running at 130% of the 10-year average number of fires and 146% of the 10-year average acres burned, so this floor is likely to rise substantially.
